Unlike the configuration model, the result is always simple, with no doubled edges or self-loops." width="100%"} Creates one node per entry of `degree_sequence`, and node `i` gets exactly `degree_sequence[i]` neighbors, with no self-loops or parallel edges. That is the difference from `configuration_model()`, which allows both and so matches the degrees only as a multigraph. Edges are added one at a time between nodes that still have free stubs, and a candidate pair `(u, v)` is accepted with probability `1 - d_u * d_v / (4 * m)`, where `d` is the degree and `m` the number of edges. Damping pairs of high-degree nodes this way makes the result nearly uniform over all simple graphs with these degrees (the algorithm of Bayati, Kim and Saberi). An attempt occasionally gets stuck with stubs that can't be joined, so up to `tries=` attempts are made. The process follows NetworkX's `random_degree_sequence_graph()`. In a directed graph every edge points from the earlier-created node to the later one. The graph is appended without touching or connecting to existing nodes, and the whole construction is recorded as a single step. Random degree-sequence graphs are useful for: - null models that keep every node's degree, e.g. to test whether clustering or assortativity is more than the degrees explain - random graphs that match an observed network's degrees exactly - comparing against `add_havel_hakimi_graph()`, the deterministic realization ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [degree_sequence]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Degree of each new node, as a list of non-negative integers. The sum must be even. [tries]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[10]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Maximum number of attempts. Default is `10`. Must be at least `1`. Small, dense sequences get stuck more often (for `[5, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1]`, about two attempts in three), so they may need more. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Integer seed for the random number generator. The same `seed=` with the same other arguments always gives the same graph. If `None` (default), the graph differs on every call. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `type` attribute of every new node. If `None` (default), no `type` attribute is set. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), each new node is labelled with its node ID as a string; a label that is already used raises `ValueError` before anything is added. If `False`, the nodes are left unlabelled. [rel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `rel` attribute of every new edge. If `None` (default), no `rel` attribute is set. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `degree_sequence=` contains a negative entry or is not graphical, `tries=` is less than `1`, or every attempt gets stuck. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Every node gets its degree, and there are no self-loops or parallel edges: ::: {#b0a64a94 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec degrees = [4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1] graph = ec.Graph().add_random_degree_sequence_graph(degrees, seed=3) [graph.get_degree(v) for v in sorted(graph.get_node_ids())] == degrees, graph.is_simple() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (True, True) ``` ::: ::: Unlike `add_havel_hakimi_graph()`, which joins the highest-degree nodes to each other, a random realization is close to neutral in its degree mixing: ::: {#4479ce1d .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} degrees = [5] * 10 + [2] * 40 random_graph = ec.Graph().add_random_degree_sequence_graph(degrees, seed=3) hh_graph = ec.Graph().add_havel_hakimi_graph(degrees) ( round(random_graph.degree_pearson_correlation_coefficient(), 2), round(hh_graph.degree_pearson_correlation_coefficient(), 2), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (-0.3, 1.0) ``` ::: :::
